The weighbridge at Kesterby market was laid down in 1871 and gave no trouble until 1902. In that year the carriers began to complain. A load weighed on the market bridge and weighed again at the railway yard, four miles down the valley, came to two different figures, and the yard’s was always the higher — by thirty to forty pounds in a load of half a ton. What made the complaint hard to credit was the exception: on Thursdays the two tickets agreed exactly, and on Thursdays alone.

The market committee tried three explanations and tested all three. The first was that the railway’s bridge, not Kesterby’s, was out of adjustment; the inspector of weights and measures came out with sealed standards and found the yard’s bridge true to four ounces. The second was that carts were being driven up with a wheel off the platform; a cart was squared on the deck by two men with a plumb line and weighed light exactly as before. The third was that the clerk read the beam in haste; a load of pig iron of a known weight was left on the bridge for an hour and read by three men in turn, and it weighed light for all three.

Hannah Rowe took over the bridge’s book in 1909 and kept a column nobody had asked her for. Every morning she wrote down the depth of water standing in the pit. The pit is the chamber under the platform that carries the knife-edges on which the whole train of levers rests, and it drains by a culvert into the Lissel brook. Two or three inches of water stood in it on most days. On Thursdays it was dry.

The Kesterby brewery mashed on Thursdays, and mashing meant drawing the brook down through the brewery’s intake for six hours together. With the brook low the culvert ran free and the pit drained. On every other day the brook stood high enough to back the culvert up, and the water in the pit floated the timber shoring against the underside of the platform, carrying a part of the load that should have gone down on to the knife-edges. Thursday had never been the odd day. Thursday was the only day that was right.

Rowe then set the brewery’s mash book beside the bridge’s book for eleven years. The four Tuesdays in 1911 on which the brewery mashed early, to fill a coronation order, are four Tuesdays on which the bridge weighed true. The six weeks after the malthouse fire, when no mash was made at all, contain no true day whatever, Thursdays included. A flap valve was fitted to the mouth of the culvert in 1921, and the two tickets have agreed since.

The parish of Oustry held its fair in the second week of September until 1788, and in the first week of May from 1789 onward. No parish record gives a reason for the change, and two accounts of it survive that do not agree.

The first is a note in the hand of the curate, Abbé Tessier, written on the flyleaf of a baptismal register. The September fair, he says, was given up after the sickness among the cattle, and May was chosen because it falls before the hill pastures are let. The second account is in the pleadings of a lawsuit brought in 1802 by a miller, Claude Barral, against the former seigneurial agent. Barral swears that the date was moved so that the fair should fall while the wool caravan from the south was still on the road, and that the agent, who took a due on every fleece sold at Oustry, had the moving of it.

Each account has something against it. Tessier’s note is undated, and the writing is the writing of his old age — he died in 1821 — so it may have been set down thirty years after the thing it describes. The veterinary returns for the district record no sickness among cattle in those years, though they are incomplete for 1787 and 1788. Barral, for his part, gave his testimony in a suit he stood to win, against a man whose office had been abolished and who did not appear to answer him; the court took the testimony without calling a single witness to it. Neither man is a liar on the face of things. Neither is a witness anyone would have chosen.

The document that would have decided the question did exist. The parish’s deliberation book, in which the assembly entered the reasons for its acts, ran unbroken from 1752, and the removal of the fair would have been entered there. It was burned with the district’s seigneurial papers in the autumn of 1794. The inventory drawn up before the burning lists the book by its title and gives nothing of its contents.

What is left is a choice between two accounts almost equally weak, and the honest course is to say so. One historian may prefer Tessier, on the ground that a man writing a private note has less to gain by it. Another may prefer Barral, on the ground that a man swearing to a date in court has more to lose. Neither preference is evidence, and the question stands where it stood.

The painted ceiling of the Salle des Toiles at Verrey was laid in 1690 in distemper over a thin coat of size, and the size holds the painter’s charcoal setting-out. Until the middle of the last century that setting-out could be read. Where the distemper had worn thin — which was most of the north slope — a lamp held almost flat to the plaster brought up the charcoal lines underneath, and a survey made in 1931 photographed thirty-one tally marks along the beams, the marks by which the work had been divided among the men who did it.

Mireille Danet cleaned the ceiling between 1958 and 1963, and her method was the most cautious then available. She used no solvent of any kind. The dirt was taken off with dry bread-crumb and a soft rubber, worked a hand’s breadth from the plaster, and it was close work: she and two assistants spent five years on a surface a mason would have limewashed in a fortnight. Her refusal of solvents was principled and she published it. A solvent, she argued, goes in and alters what lies under the surface, and nobody can see what it is doing while it does it.

What bread-crumb does is take away the surface itself. In the worn passages of the north slope there was very little distemper left to lose, and the crumbing lifted what there was along with the dirt. The charcoal beneath was not touched; what went was the thin, translucent film through which it had been legible in raking light. After 1963 the lamp brings up nothing on the north slope. Of the thirty-one tally marks photographed in 1931, fourteen could not be found again.

Her caution was real and it was aimed at the wrong danger. She guarded the layer under the surface against a method that would have reached it, and destroyed the reading of that layer with a method that could not reach it at all. The setting-out is the only record of how a ceiling of that size was planned and shared out; the painted face of it, which she saved, is a thing anyone can photograph in an afternoon.

How much was lost altogether cannot be stated, and it is worth saying why not. The 1931 survey covers the west half of the ceiling and no more. Tova kept the table. It hung on the inside of the shed door at the Skaal crossing, a printed sheet from the Vin almanac giving the minute of slack water for every day of the year, and her uncle Ferd ran the ferry by it.

The sheet was computed for the harbour mouth at Vin, eleven miles north. Nobody had ever said otherwise; it was printed at the head of the sheet in type smaller than the figures. What Tova did, in the winter she turned fourteen, was keep a column of her own. The eddy under the east pier turns over at slack water — it stands, goes glassy, and then turns the other way, and a person watching for it can put a minute to it. She wrote her minute down every morning from October to March, and then set her column beside the printed one. The crossing ran later than Vin by twenty-two minutes: never less than nineteen, never more than twenty-five.

She took it to Ferd, who read the two columns down twice and did not dispute a figure of them. Then he said that the sheet was printed, and that a printed sheet was the same sheet for everyone. If the ferry went out on a printed minute and the minute was wrong, the fault was the almanac’s. If it went out on a chalked minute, the fault was the ferry’s, and the chalk would be hers.

Tova did not argue with that, and she did not rub the sheet out either. She chalked her minute on the door each morning beside the printed one, in the same size of figure, with both of them there to be read together. Ferd said nothing about it and went out, most mornings that spring, on the chalk.

In March she copied three winters of her column into a fair hand and sent it to the compiler at Vin, with a note saying that his table was not wrong — that it was being read eleven miles from where it had been computed, and that the difference was twenty-two minutes and would be the same next year.

Anyone who has stood in the machine house of the Kaltbrunn funicular has heard the note. It is low, steady, somewhere near the bottom of a woman’s voice, and it comes up out of the haul rope and not out of the machinery. Two explanations were current for sixty years. One was the wind, which draws across the rope where it leaves the house and can be heard doing it. The other was the sheaves, the grooved wheels that carry the rope up the incline, which turn at a rate that could plausibly set up the pitch.

Emil Perc recorded the note through the season of 1974, at the same place in the house, and set the pitch he measured against three other quantities: the wind speed at the head of the incline, the turning rate of the sheaves, and the pull on the rope, which can be read directly at the counterweight. The note ignores the first two. On days with no wind it is there; at every speed the sheaves run it is the same note. Against the pull it moves exactly, and it moves in the way that settles the matter: the pitch rises as the square root of the pull, which is the law a stretched string obeys and the law nothing else in the building obeys. The rope is sounding as a string sounds, and the sixty-year argument is over.

Settling it produced a second thing that Perc had not gone looking for. A set of recordings had been made in 1970, for another purpose, in the same house and at the same place. The note on those is higher than anything in his own season, and by the square-root law the difference is a pull about nine parts in a hundred greater in 1970 than in 1974. The rope’s tension had drifted down over four years, and nobody had known, because nobody had a reason to read the counterweight twice.

Why it drifted, Perc does not say, and he is careful about not saying it. Two causes will produce that figure. The guides on the counterweight may be binding, so that a part of the weight is standing on the guides instead of hanging on the rope. Or the lay of the rope may be closing up with use, which lengthens it slightly and lets the counterweight down. His recordings cannot separate the two, since both appear only as a lower pull, and the measurement that would separate them — a gauge on the rope itself, above and below the guides — has never been fitted at Kaltbrunn.

The Braithe town archive mends torn leaves with gummed linen tape, and has done since 1961. The practice should stop, and there are two reasons, of which the second is much the graver.

The first is what the adhesive does. It does not stay where it is put. It travels into the fibres of the leaf on either side of the tape, and in thirty years or so it stains a band about a centimetre wide down each side of the tear. The archive has the material to check this on its own shelves: leaves torn and taped in 1961 can be set against leaves torn in the same decade and never taped, and the difference is not arguable. A tear runs where a leaf is folded and handled, which is to say through the middle of the written page, and the stained band is exactly the part of the page a reader has come for. In the Braithe rate books that part is a column of sums in a cramped nineteenth-century hand, and a stain across a figure can turn a three into an eight.

The second reason is that a mend is a claim. A torn leaf can be brought together at more than one angle, and the angle decides what the words at the tear are. Where a tear passes through a line of writing, one closing may give “the mill at Harrow bridge” and another “the mill at Harrow, bridge repaired”; both are legible, both are possible, and until the leaf is fixed both are available to whoever reads it next. Tape fixes one of them and throws the other away, and it does so silently — the reader who comes after sees a mended page and not a decision.

There is one case where a mend is right, and it should be stated plainly rather than left for someone to discover as an exception. A leaf already in fragments has to be held in some order or it is lost altogether. There the fragments should be supported — on a hinge that can be taken off again, and with a note in the file saying who put them in that order and on what grounds.

Everywhere else the answer is to stop. A torn leaf can be interleaved and boxed flat, which costs less than tape, takes an afternoon to learn, and leaves the next reader with the same page the last one had.
